title: Assembly: Machine Code with Names
summary: Assembly language writes each machine instruction as a short name - mov, add, jmp - with labels instead of addresses. An assembler translates it, almost one line to one instruction, into machine code. So assembly is not binary, but it is the thinnest possible layer over it, different for every CPU family.
markdown:
## Is assembly just binary? Not quite, but almost. **Assembly language** is machine code written so that people can read it: | Machine code (hex) | Assembly | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `B8 2A 00 00 00` | `mov eax, 42` | put 42 into register eax | | `01 D8` | `add eax, ebx` | eax = eax + ebx | | `C3` | `ret` | return | Each line of assembly is (nearly always) **exactly one machine instruction**. Nothing is added, nothing is hidden: you choose every register and every instruction yourself. The names are called **mnemonics** (memory aids): `mov` for move, `jmp` for jump, `cmp` for compare. A program called an **assembler** reads the text and writes the bytes. It is a translator, but a very direct one - closer to looking words up in a dictionary than to understanding sentences. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Assembly text
mov eax, 42
ret"] -->|assembler| M["Machine code
B8 2A 00 00 00 C3"] -->|loaded into memory| C["CPU runs it"] ``` ## What the assembler does for you Besides turning names into numbers, an assembler handles the jobs that make raw machine code miserable (4.05): - **Labels**: you write `loop:` before an instruction and `jmp loop` elsewhere; the assembler works out the address. Add an instruction in the middle and it recalculates every address for you. - **Data**: `message: db "Hello", 10` puts those bytes in the program and lets you refer to them by name. - **Constants and comments**: `length equ 6`, and anything after `;` is a note for people. Here is the tiny computer's countdown from 4.04 in an assembly language for that machine, and the numbers an assembler would produce: ``` LOAD counter ; cell 0: 106 top: JUMPZ done ; cell 1: 605 SUB one ; cell 2: 307 STORE counter ; cell 3: 406 JUMP top ; cell 4: 501 done: HALT ; cell 5: 000 counter: 3 ; cell 6: the number 3 one: 1 ; cell 7: the number 1 ``` `top`, `done`, `counter` and `one` are labels; the assembler works out which cell each one names (`counter` is cell 6, so `LOAD counter` becomes 106) and puts the data right after the code. You will write exactly this assembler in this milestone's project. ## Real x86-64 assembly A complete Linux program in x86-64 assembly (NASM syntax, as the Assembly course uses) that prints a message and exits: ```nasm global _start section .data message: db "Hello from assembly", 10 ; the bytes of the text, then a new line length equ $ - message ; how many bytes that was section .text _start: mov eax, 1 ; system call 1: write mov edi, 1 ; to standard output lea rsi, [rel message] ; these bytes mov edx, length ; this many of them syscall ; ask the operating system mov eax, 60 ; system call 60: exit xor edi, edi ; with code 0 syscall ``` Press **Run**: this is real assembly, assembled with NASM and run on a Linux machine. Every line under `_start` is one instruction. Notice how printing works at this level: there is no `print`. The program puts the number of the request (1 means "write"), where to write, the address of the bytes and their count into registers, and asks the operating system with `syscall` (lesson 6.04). ## One assembly per CPU family Because assembly is just machine code with names, there is a different assembly language for every instruction set: x86-64 assembly, ARM64 assembly, RISC-V assembly. The same "add two registers" is: | CPU | Assembly | |---|---| | x86-64 | `add eax, ebx` | | ARM64 | `add w0, w0, w1` | | RISC-V | `add a0, a0, a1` | And even for one CPU there can be several spellings (NASM, GNU, MASM syntax), all producing the same bytes. ## Who writes assembly today? Almost nobody writes whole programs in it any more - compilers (5.03) produce faster code than most people would write by hand. But assembly is still essential for: - understanding what a program really does: crashes, performance, security; - the first instructions that run when a computer starts (6.05), and parts of operating systems; - tight loops in video codecs, cryptography and game engines; - reading what a compiler made from your code. > [!info] Who wrote the first assembly language? > **Kathleen Booth** designed an assembly language for the ARC computer in London around 1947. In 1949 **David Wheeler**'s "initial orders" for EDSAC (1.03) let programmers write instructions as letters and decimal numbers, which the machine translated as it loaded them. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is the relationship between assembly and machine code? - Assembly is the same as binary + Each line is one instruction, written as a name - Assembly is a high-level language like Python > Nearly every assembly line is one machine instruction written as a name instead of numbers, so an assembler translates it almost one to one. ? What does a label like loop: give the programmer? - A comment for the reader - A new instruction + A name for an address > The assembler works out the address and keeps it up to date: no more recalculating jump addresses by hand. ? Why is there no single assembly language? - People never agreed on a syntax + Each CPU family has its own instructions - Assembly is not used any more > x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V each have their own instructions, so each has its own assembly. ```
